summary:
Bretagne stands under the national framework of France. Identity-document law, anti-discrimination provisions, criminal law, the prison-placement rules and the marriage statute apply across the country's regions without territorial variation, and no source in the inventory records a Bretagne-specific finding on transgender travellers.

The documented risks concentrate in two settings: custody and the border. In ordinary movement through accommodation, services and public space, France's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition.

Prison placement follows the sex inscribed on the detainee's identity documents. Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code requires men and women to be held in separate establishments, and the vast majority of trans women, most of whom have not undergone sex-reassignment surgery, carry documents marked male and are consequently held in men's facilities. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 records a trans woman recalling inmates shouting "We don't want any women here!" and threatening violence against her.

Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, states that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers the most in French prisons. The same feature describes the case of Kara B., a trans American woman, held in what the controller-general called worrying conditions.

The CGLPL, France's national preventive mechanism against torture, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, following its opinion of 30 June 2010. It found serious violations of the fundamental rights of trans detainees persisting in adult prisons. No comparable violations were noted in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres. The review covered the situations of roughly forty trans detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits to the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station.

The CGLPL told the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a further opinion was needed because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because its remit now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

Placement remains contested in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained in connection with opposition to the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was raised in oral question no. 219 addressed to the Keeper of the Seals in the French National Assembly, which argued that the prison system is unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees. Placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women report being questioned publicly about their identity documents. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of questioning by French border police at the airport, conducted in front of other travellers.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. The decision cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline is the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013. CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.
tangentialFactors:
The CGLPL's two opinions bracket a decade of enforcement failure. The 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, and the 2021 opinion records serious violations continuing in adult prisons despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform. The reform changed documents and terminology without changing custody practice, which remains a facility-by-facility improvisation rather than a statutory rule.

The inspection picture is uneven by setting. The same CGLPL review that found serious violations in adult prisons recorded none in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres. This distinction matters to a visitor because it separates the highest-risk custodial setting, the men's prison, from health and youth detention environments, where the evidence of harm is thinner.

The inspection visits that ground the 2021 opinion took place at four adult prisons and one central police station, none of them in Bretagne. The region therefore has no recorded custodial inspection finding for trans detainees in the available sources, and the national pattern cannot be read as local documentation.

Border friction is documented in one first-person account rather than in an official finding. Giovanna Rincon's 2017 StreetPress description of public document questioning at an airport illustrates the pattern but carries the weight of a single testimony.

The discrimination benchmark France's rights defender relies on, 64% reporting identity-related discrimination in the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, is a population-level figure and not a traveller exposure rate.
localsOnly:
Where a trans woman is held in French custody is decided by the gender inscribed on her identity documents, and each establishment improvises: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. Treatment varies between establishments, and the accounts collected in the BuzzFeed News feature describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

Trans detainees remain the group identified by the national custodial-inspection authority as suffering most in prison. Adeline Hazan's characterisation predates the 2021 opinion and is consistent with it.

The 2021 opinion found structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention, resting on a decade of correspondence from detained trans people. Isolation is recorded not as a protection but as a source of harm, and the practice was still in use in 2025 in the Louna case at Tarbes.

The Défenseur des droits' framework decision confirms persistent fundamental-rights violations on the basis of case files and association testimony, and supplies official guidance for service providers.

Legal gender recognition, in force in its 2016 form, is not described as a barrier in the sources reviewed here; the barrier documented is what happens after recognition, when placement still tracks the old document.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents any Bretagne-specific inspection, casework, detention incident or police encounter. The custodial inspections cited in the CGLPL opinion took place elsewhere in France, and the region-level position is therefore an extension of the national framework rather than a local finding.

The text of the Défenseur des droits' framework decision is not reproduced in the inventory. The extent of its coverage for visitors, and the specific guidance it gives service providers, is unresolved here.

Louna's placement outcome is unresolved. The source establishes that she has been held in a men's prison in isolation since October 2024 and that her case was raised in the National Assembly, but it does not record any ruling on her placement.

The sources do not address gender-affirming care access in custody, access to hormone therapy while detained, or the interaction between the 2016 gender-recognition procedure and entry to the country. No material on visitor-facing healthcare availability in the region is present in the inventory.

The partner-recognition baseline rests on 2013 reporting, and no post-2013 development on marriage or partner recognition is sourced here. Nor is any source available on visa or entry screening criteria for transgender travellers beyond the single 2017 border account.
